summary: An introduction to describing data and using samples to make claims about a population, from graphs and averages to confidence intervals and regression.

topics.title: Samples and data displays
topics.description: Sampling methods, sources of bias, and frequency distributions connect the way data are collected with what a graph can reasonably show.

topics.title: Center and variation
topics.description: Means, medians, percentiles, and measures of spread describe both a typical observation and how widely observations vary.

topics.title: Probability and distributions
topics.description: Basic probability leads to discrete distributions, binomial counts, and the normal distribution. Standard scores locate an observation relative to a distribution's center and spread.

topics.title: Sampling distributions and intervals
topics.description: Sampling distributions explain why estimates vary between samples. Confidence intervals and margin of error turn that variation into estimates of population means and proportions.

topics.title: Hypothesis tests
topics.description: Tests of means, proportions, and differences between groups compare observed data with a stated population claim. Test statistics and probability values support conclusions about that claim.

topics.title: Correlation and regression
topics.description: Scatterplots, correlation, and fitted lines describe relationships between two variables. The coefficient of determination summarizes the variation accounted for by a linear fit.

sourceNote: Historical Statistics syllabus, including its topic schedule and stated learning outcomes; original assignment work is sparsely preserved.

summary: Angles, triangles, and periodic functions, followed by alternative ways to describe position and motion using polar coordinates, complex numbers, and vectors.

topics.title: Angles and the unit circle
topics.description: Degree and radian measures connect triangle ratios with coordinates on the unit circle. This extends trigonometric functions beyond acute angles.

topics.title: Function graphs and inverses
topics.description: Sine, cosine, and the other trigonometric graphs describe periodic behavior. Transformations change their size, period, and position; inverse functions recover angles within a chosen range.

topics.title: Identities and equations
topics.description: Trigonometric identities express the same quantity in different forms. They support simplification and solving equations while keeping track of all permitted angles.

topics.title: Triangle applications
topics.description: Right-triangle methods and the laws of sines and cosines recover unknown sides and angles, including triangles that do not contain a right angle.

topics.title: Parametric and polar curves
topics.description: Parametric equations describe coordinates through a shared parameter. Polar coordinates use distance and angle.

topics.title: Complex numbers and vectors
topics.description: Polar form makes complex multiplication and roots geometric. Vectors describe quantities with both magnitude and direction.

sourceNote: Saved historical Canvas syllabus and its learning outcomes for McKeague and Turner, Trigonometry, eighth edition.

summary: Single-variable change and accumulation: limits lead to derivatives, derivatives support local analysis and optimization, and integrals connect accumulated quantities with rates.

topics.title: Chapter 2: Limits and continuity
topics.description: Limits describe a function's behavior near an input, even when direct substitution fails. Continuity connects that nearby behavior with the actual function value.

topics.title: Chapter 3: Derivatives
topics.description: The derivative begins as a limit of slopes and becomes a collection of differentiation rules. Implicit and logarithmic differentiation extend those rules to less direct relationships.

topics.title: Rates and local approximation
topics.description: Related-rates problems connect quantities changing together. Linear approximation uses a tangent line to estimate nearby values.

topics.title: Chapter 4: Function behavior and optimization
topics.description: Critical points, the mean value theorem, and derivative signs explain extrema and graph shape. Applications include optimization, indeterminate limits, and Newton's method for approximate roots.

topics.title: Chapter 5: Integrals and accumulation
topics.description: Antiderivatives and definite integrals connect area and accumulated change. The fundamental theorem of calculus links integration with differentiation, followed by substitution.

sourceNote: Saved Fall 2023 Canvas module scope: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, eighth edition, Chapters 2–5.

summary: Integration techniques, improper integrals and arc length lead into sequences, series and polynomial approximation.

topics.title: Integration by parts and trigonometric integrals
topics.description: Integration by parts reverses the product rule. Trigonometric identities turn products and powers of sine and cosine into forms that can be integrated.

topics.title: Trigonometric substitution and partial fractions
topics.description: Trigonometric substitutions simplify particular square-root expressions. Partial fractions split rational functions into simpler terms with recognizable antiderivatives.

topics.title: Improper integrals and arc length
topics.description: Limits determine whether an integral with an infinite interval or unbounded integrand converges. Arc-length calculations accumulate the small distances along a curve.

topics.title: Chapter 11: Sequences and series
topics.description: Sequence limits distinguish individual terms from their accumulated sum. Geometric, telescoping and alternating series illustrate different ways to test convergence.

topics.title: Power series and Taylor approximation
topics.description: Power-series work asks where an infinite polynomial converges, including its endpoints. Taylor polynomials approximate functions near a chosen center, with error estimates controlling the approximation.

sourceNote: Retained integration, arc-length, Chapter 11 and exam-review notes, with their retrospective topic map; a complete original syllabus or final scope is not preserved.

summary: Vectors and curves describe geometry and motion in space; partial derivatives extend differentiation to functions of several variables.

topics.title: 12.1 · Coordinates, distances and spheres
topics.description: Locate points and octants in three dimensions, calculate distances, and describe spheres and their intersections with coordinate planes.

topics.title: 12.2 · Vectors and direction
topics.description: Vector components describe displacement. Magnitude measures its size, and a unit vector preserves its direction with length one.

topics.title: 12.3 · Dot products and projections
topics.description: The dot product connects vector components with angles and perpendicularity. Projections resolve one vector along the direction of another.

topics.title: 12.4 · Cross products and area
topics.description: A cross product produces a vector perpendicular to two given vectors. Its magnitude gives parallelogram area.

topics.title: 12.5 · Lines and planes
topics.description: Parametric lines and plane equations describe sets of points in space. Intersections and angles compare their positions and directions.

topics.title: 13.1–13.2 · Vector functions and space curves
topics.description: A vector-valued function traces a curve through space. Domains, limits and componentwise derivatives describe its behavior and give tangent lines.

topics.title: 13.3 · Arc length and curvature
topics.description: Integrating speed measures distance along a curve. Tangent and normal vectors describe its turning, while curvature and osculating circles quantify that turn locally.

topics.title: 13.4 · Motion in space
topics.description: Position, velocity, acceleration and speed describe motion. Initial conditions determine a particular trajectory, including projectile motion.

topics.title: 14.3 · Partial derivatives and rates
topics.description: A partial derivative measures change in one input while holding the others fixed. Rates, units and implicit differentiation describe change in multivariable relationships.

topics.title: 14.3 · Higher and mixed partial derivatives
topics.description: Repeated differentiation gives second and higher partial derivatives. Clairaut’s theorem gives conditions for interchanging mixed derivatives; substitution checks whether a function satisfies a partial differential equation.

sourceNote: Historical Chapter 12 and 13 review problems and Chapter 14.3 notes. Original syllabus and later module scope are not retained; the empty 14.6 file and generated readiness questions do not establish later historical coverage.

summary: A foundation in mathematical reasoning and finite structures, combining logic and induction with counting and probability.

topics.title: Logic and formal statements
topics.description: Propositions, logical connectives, and quantified statements turn informal claims into expressions with precise truth conditions.

topics.title: Proof and induction
topics.description: Proof methods justify a conclusion from stated assumptions. Mathematical induction proves a sequence of claims by establishing a starting case and a step from one case to the next.

topics.title: Counting
topics.description: Counting rules distinguish ordered arrangements from unordered selections. They organize finite possibilities before a probability or combinatorial argument is attempted.

topics.title: Finite probability
topics.description: Sample spaces and events connect counting with chance. Finite probability models make the choice of outcomes and assumptions explicit.

topics.title: Numbers and representations
topics.description: Different number representations encode the same value in different forms.

sourceNote: Saved historical Canvas syllabus: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, 2025 release, with Chapters 1, 5, 6 and 7 listed as the main coverage.

summary: The introductory course develops the connection between solving linear systems, working with matrices, and understanding vector spaces and transformations.

topics.title: Systems and matrices
topics.description: Systems of linear equations become matrix problems. Matrix operations and determinants provide tools for describing solutions and invertibility.

topics.title: Vector spaces and bases
topics.description: Span and linear independence describe what a collection of vectors can generate. Bases and dimension identify a minimal coordinate system for a space.

topics.title: Linear transformations
topics.description: Linear transformations preserve addition and scalar multiplication. Their matrix representations connect geometric actions with calculations.

topics.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
topics.description: Eigenvectors identify directions preserved by a transformation, with eigenvalues giving the scaling along those directions.

topics.title: Orthogonality and least squares
topics.description: Perpendicular vectors and projections support approximation. Least squares finds a best fit when a system does not have an exact solution.

sourceNote: Saved Spring 2026 introductory-course syllabus, using Lay, Linear Algebra and Its Applications, sixth edition; distinct from the later Bretscher theory course.

summary: Proof-based work on integers, from divisibility and the Euclidean algorithm to modular arithmetic, quadratic residues, and elementary cryptography.

topics.title: Proof, divisibility and greatest common divisors
topics.description: Direct arguments and induction establish facts about integers. The Euclidean algorithm computes a greatest common divisor and connects it with integer linear combinations.

topics.title: Primes and Diophantine equations
topics.description: Prime factorization describes the multiplicative structure of integers. Linear Diophantine equations ask when an equation has integer solutions and how to describe all of them.

topics.title: Congruences and the Chinese remainder theorem
topics.description: Congruences compare integers by their remainders. The Chinese remainder theorem combines several modular conditions into a single solution description.

topics.title: Fermat, Euler and arithmetic functions
topics.description: Fermat's, Euler's, and Wilson's theorems connect powers and factorials with modular arithmetic. Arithmetic functions track properties such as the number of residues relatively prime to a modulus.

topics.title: Orders and primitive roots
topics.description: The order of a residue records when its repeated powers return to one. Primitive roots generate the invertible residues for moduli where such generators exist.

topics.title: Quadratic residues and reciprocity
topics.description: Quadratic residues identify which congruences have square roots. Euler's criterion, Legendre symbols, and quadratic reciprocity turn those existence questions into structured calculations and proofs.

sourceNote: Saved historical weekly schedule and final-scope summary, supported by Homework 1–10; the schedule also includes a final cryptography reading.

summary: The Koch snowflake connects repeated geometric construction with finite area, unbounded perimeter and a non-integer similarity dimension.

topics.title: The Koch construction
topics.description: Each stage replaces every line segment with four shorter segments. Repeating the same geometric rule produces increasing detail while preserving a recognizable overall shape.

topics.title: Perimeter and area
topics.description: The segment count and segment length form geometric sequences. Their combined effect makes the perimeter grow without bound even as the total added area approaches a finite limit.

topics.title: Self-similarity and dimension
topics.description: Smaller copies reproduce the construction at a reduced scale. Similarity dimension relates the number of copies to their scale factor, extending the usual integer dimensions of lines and surfaces.

topics.title: Presenting a mathematical argument
topics.description: The presentation organizes the construction, formulas and limiting argument for an audience. Indexing choices clarify how each stage changes the perimeter and area.

sourceNote: Saved Koch-snowflake talk drafts, slides and preparation notes; this reflects the preserved presentation rather than a full seminar syllabus.

summary: Differential equations connect a rule for change with the functions that obey it, from first-order models to second- and higher-order linear equations.

topics.title: Equations, solutions and direction fields
topics.description: Order and linearity classify differential equations. Substitution checks a proposed solution, while direction fields and initial values describe how a particular solution behaves.

topics.title: First-order solution methods
topics.description: Separation of variables, integrating factors, exact equations, and substitutions apply to different equation structures. Each method transforms the equation into a form that can be integrated.

topics.title: Models and equilibrium behavior
topics.description: Population, mixing, and motion models express changing quantities through differential equations. Equilibria and phase-line signs explain long-term behavior without requiring an explicit formula.

topics.title: Existence, uniqueness and solution intervals
topics.description: Conditions on an equation determine where an initial-value problem has a solution and whether that solution is unique. Singular coefficients and domain restrictions limit the interval being considered.

topics.title: Second-order linear equations
topics.description: Superposition and independent solutions describe the homogeneous solution family. Characteristic roots produce real, repeated, or oscillatory solution forms for constant-coefficient equations.

topics.title: Forcing terms and higher-order equations
topics.description: Undetermined coefficients and variation of parameters construct particular solutions of nonhomogeneous equations. Higher-order equations and order reduction extend these methods.

sourceNote: Boyce, DiPrima and Meade, eleventh edition; saved Homework 1–10 prompts and course source index, spanning Chapters 1–3 and Sections 4.1–4.2.

summary: Finite probability begins with counting outcomes, then adds conditional information, independence, and numerical summaries of discrete random variables.

topics.title: Chapter 1: Counting outcomes
topics.description: Product rules, permutations, and combinations distinguish ordered arrangements from selections. Restrictions and repeated categories change which outcomes should be counted.

topics.title: Chapter 2: Events and probability
topics.description: Sample spaces, complements, unions, and intersections give events a precise structure. Inclusion–exclusion accounts for overlaps when probabilities or outcome counts are combined.

topics.title: Chapter 3: Conditioning and Bayes
topics.description: Conditional probability updates the relevant sample space after information is supplied. Multiplication, total probability, and Bayes's formula connect an observation with its possible sources.

topics.title: Independence
topics.description: Independence asks whether learning one event changes another's probability. The course distinguishes pairwise independence from mutual independence among three events.

topics.title: Chapter 4: Discrete random variables
topics.description: Probability mass and cumulative distribution functions describe the values of a random variable. Expectation and variance summarize its center and spread, including after scaling or shifting.

topics.title: Bernoulli and binomial models
topics.description: Bernoulli variables encode a single success or failure; binomial variables count successes in independent repeated trials.

sourceNote: Saved Ross, A First Course in Probability, tenth-edition assignments and confirmed cumulative scope through Section 4.6; a separate later reading introduces Poisson variables.

summary: Continuous random variables connect probability with integration, normal approximation and exponential waiting-time models.

topics.title: Continuous densities and cumulative distributions
topics.description: A density assigns probability through area over an interval. Cumulative distribution functions accumulate that area and help determine unknown normalizing constants or cutoffs.

topics.title: Expectation, variance and transformations
topics.description: Integrals compute averages and spread for continuous variables. Transformations connect a new variable's distribution or expected value with the original model.

topics.title: Uniform and normal distributions
topics.description: Uniform models spread density evenly across an interval. Normal models use a center and standard deviation, with standardization and table lookup converting values into probabilities and percentiles.

topics.title: Binomial limits and normal approximation
topics.description: The law of large numbers concerns the stability of sample proportions, while the central limit theorem describes their approximate distribution. Continuity corrections connect discrete binomial counts with normal areas.

topics.title: Exponential waiting times
topics.description: Exponential models describe nonnegative waiting times through a rate. Survival probabilities, hazard, and memorylessness explain how waiting already completed affects the remaining wait.

sourceNote: Saved Canvas assignment rows, exact Ross tenth-edition Chapter 5 prompts and recovered midterm questions; preserved assigned scope is Sections 5.1–5.5.

summary: The later theory course revisits matrices through linear maps and abstract spaces, emphasizing bases, coordinates, kernels, images, and the structure behind computations.

topics.title: Chapter 1: Linear systems and elimination
topics.description: Gauss–Jordan elimination exposes the possible solutions of a linear system. Matrix algebra packages these calculations and connects them with invertibility.

topics.title: Chapter 2: Transformations and geometry
topics.description: Reflections, rotations, and projections make linear maps concrete. Matrix multiplication represents composition, and inverse matrices reverse invertible transformations.

topics.title: Chapter 3: Subspaces, bases and coordinates
topics.description: Kernels and images identify the inputs sent to zero and the outputs a map can reach. Independence, bases, dimension, and coordinates describe these spaces without tying them to one particular spanning list.

topics.title: Chapter 4: General linear spaces
topics.description: Linear-space ideas extend to polynomials, matrices, and other objects. Isomorphisms, transformation matrices, and changes of basis compare different coordinate descriptions of the same underlying map.

topics.title: Chapter 5: Orthogonality
topics.description: Orthogonal projections, orthonormal bases, the Gram–Schmidt procedure and QR factorization connect perpendicularity with coordinate construction and matrix decomposition.

topics.title: Chapters 6–7: Determinants and eigenvectors
topics.description: Determinants connect matrices with geometry. Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and diagonalization simplify a transformation by finding directions it preserves.

sourceNote: Fall 2026 Bretscher fifth-edition syllabus and saved assignments through Section 4.2; Chapters 5–7 are later syllabus coverage, distinct from the preserved assigned work.

summary: Regression work connects fitted equations with geometry, uncertainty, and interpretation. R-based assignments develop simple and multiple regression, model comparisons, categorical predictors, and interactions.

topics.title: Least squares and regression geometry
topics.description: Least squares chooses coefficients by minimizing squared residuals. Fitted values, residuals, residual standard error, and explained variation describe what the resulting line or plane captures.

topics.title: Multiple regression and coefficient meaning
topics.description: Multiple regression estimates a predictor's association with the response while holding other included predictors fixed. Partial versus marginal slopes and standardized coefficients change how a reported effect should be interpreted.

topics.title: Assumptions and interval estimates
topics.description: The error model supplies assumptions for inference from a sample to a population. Confidence intervals describe uncertainty about mean relationships, while prediction intervals also include individual-response variation.

topics.title: Hypothesis tests and model comparisons
topics.description: Coefficient tests assess individual terms; overall and incremental F-tests assess groups of terms or compare nested models. Reading R output connects estimates and standard errors with the research question being tested.

topics.title: Collinearity
topics.description: Closely related predictors can make separate coefficient estimates unstable. Pairwise correlations and variance-inflation factors help identify that problem and assess changes to the model.

topics.title: Categorical predictors and interactions
topics.description: Indicator variables encode categories as model terms. Interactions allow one predictor's slope to depend on another predictor or group, requiring separate equations and conditional interpretations.

sourceNote: Saved instructor study guides, slide and Homework 1–7 records, and R labs; Fox, Applied Regression Analysis and Generalized Linear Models, third edition. The later project also requires logistic regression.
